claims.claim: Cleopatra lived closer to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid.
claims.source_checked: Rosso, Toxicology Reports 8 (2021), PMC8042289 (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8042289/); Sheisha et al., PNAS 119(37) (2022), PMC9477388 (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9477388/); NASA images-api.nasa.gov record as11-40-5903
claims.note: Rosso: 'Cleopatra VII was born at 69 BC'; 'committed suicide in August 30 BC'. NASA AS11-40-5903: Aldrin on the lunar surface, 20 July 1969. Sheisha: the Great Pyramid is the 'Khufu Pyramid'; his accession 'ranges from 2613 to 2577 BCE (1 sigma)' (14C), or 2589, 2554, or 2480 +/- 5 BCE. Even on the lowest date (Spence, reign ending c. 2453 with Year 27), the pyramid is >= 2,384 years before her birth against 2,037 years from 69 BC to AD 1969; from her death, >= 2,423 against 1,998. True as stated at second two, on every chronology given. Erdil 2025 not opened; not needed for this claim.

claims.claim: So what did the pyramid look like in her day? Not this.
claims.source_checked: Diodorus 1.63.5, Oldfather Loeb 279 (1933), archive.org/stream/diodorus-of-sicily-in-twelve-volumes.-vol.-1-loeb-279 (djvu full text); Tallet & Marouard 2014 (see 3)
claims.note: Implied claim: in the 1st c. BC the pyramid looked different from today's stepped core. Supported by claim 3's sources (casing then in place; Oldfather's note: 'the facing, which has now almost entirely disappeared'). Visual 'this' not yet cut; when it is, the picture must show the present-day pyramid with exposed core (A6). No claim Cleopatra saw it.

claims.claim: It still wore its smooth, polished outer casing.
claims.source_checked: Herodotus 2.124-125, tr. Godley, Loeb 117, archive.org/stream/herodotus01hero (djvu full text); Diodorus 1.63.5 + Oldfather n. 1 p. 217, Loeb 279 (archive.org, as in 2); Tallet & Marouard, Near Eastern Archaeology 77(1) 2014, p. 9, archive.org/stream/theharborofkhufuontheredseacoastatwadialjarfegypt
claims.note: Herodotus 2.124: 'the whole is of stone polished and most exactly fitted'; Godley's note at 2.125: the filling stones 'make the side of the pyramid a smooth inclined plane'. 'Still' in her day: Diodorus (visit 60-56 BC) 'the stones remain to this day still preserving their original position and the entire structure undecayed'. 'Casing': T&M 2014 p. 9, Tura blocks 'probably used for the external casing of the Great Pyramid, made of fine limestone'; Oldfather: 'Including the facing, which has now almost entirely disappeared'. Non-blocking: SOURCES entry 3 rests 'casing' on the NOVA interviews (not A2); replace that citation with T&M 2014 p. 9 and Oldfather's note, which both say it.

claims.claim: A Greek historian, Diodorus, visited Egypt when Cleopatra was a girl.
claims.source_checked: Diodorus 1.44.1 and 1.4.4, Oldfather intro and notes, Loeb 279 (archive.org, as in 2); Rosso 2021 PMC8042289
claims.note: 1.44.1: 'down to the One Hundred and Eightieth Olympiad, the time when we visited Egypt and the king was Ptolemy, who took the name of The New Dionysus'; Oldfather n. 2: Auletes, 'father of the famous Cleopatra' (Loeb numbers him XI; Rosso: Ptolemy XII Auletes, father of Cleopatra VII; script gives no number). 180th Olympiad = 60/59-57/56 BC; born 69 BC, she was about 9-13. 'Greek historian': 1.4.4 city of origin Agyrium in Sicily; Jerome via Oldfather, 'a writer of Greek history'.

claims.claim: He wrote that its stones were still in place.
claims.source_checked: Diodorus 1.63.2-5 + Oldfather n. 1 p. 215, Loeb 279 (archive.org, as in 2)
claims.note: 1.63.5: 'the stones remain to this day still preserving their original position'. 'Its' = the largest pyramid, built by Chemmis; Oldfather: 'Chemmis is the Cheops of Herodotus (2. 124), the Khufu of the monuments', i.e. the Great Pyramid.

claims.claim: He was told three hundred and sixty thousand men spent twenty years building it.
claims.note: 'three hundred and sixty thousand men, as they say, were employed on the undertaking, and the whole structure was scarcely completed in twenty years'. 'He was told' matches 'as they say' and marks it as report, not record (A5).

claims.claim: He wrote that an inscription listed what the workers' vegetables and laxatives cost: over sixteen hundred talents.
claims.note: 'an inscription on the larger pyramid gives the sum of money expended on it, since the writing sets forth that on vegetables and purgatives for the workmen there were paid out over sixteen hundred talents'. 'Laxatives' = Oldfather's 'purgatives'. Framed as Diodorus's report ('He wrote'), not as a surviving inscription; no 'of silver' (that is Herodotus 2.125).

claims.claim: Then, in 2013, at an ancient harbour on the Red Sea, archaeologists found papyri from the reign of the pyramid's own king, Khufu.
claims.source_checked: Tallet & Marouard, 'The Harbor of Khufu on the Red Sea Coast at Wadi al-Jarf, Egypt', NEA 77(1): 4-14 (2014), doi:10.5615/neareastarch.77.1.0004, full scan archive.org/stream/theharborofkhufuontheredseacoastatwadialjarfegypt
claims.note: p. 8: 'the 2013 campaign has led to an even more remarkable discovery ... several hundreds of papyrus fragments', 'very well dated to the end of Khufu's reign', 'Khufu's regnal Year 27'. Title and p. 6: harbour/port complex on the Red Sea coast, 'ca. 2600-2550 b.c.e.'. Khufu = the Great Pyramid's king (Sheisha 2022; Oldfather on Diodorus).

claims.claim: The oldest papyri with writing ever found in Egypt.
claims.source_checked: Tallet & Marouard 2014, p. 8 (archive.org scan, as in 8)
claims.note: 'This information makes these documents the oldest inscribed papyri that have ever been discovered in Egypt.' 'With writing' = 'inscribed' (older blank papyrus exists, so the qualifier must stay). The scope is the source's, as of 2014; I found no later source contradicting it but did not search for one.

claims.claim: Among them was the logbook of Merer's boat crew, hauling limestone from a quarry seventeen kilometres away to the pyramid.
claims.source_checked: Tallet & Marouard 2014, pp. 8-9 (archive.org scan, as in 8); Sheisha et al. 2022, PMC9477388
claims.note: T&M: 'a personal logbook that records every day activities of a team led by ... the inspector Merer', 'about 200 men'; 'transportation, on the Nile and connected canals, of stone blocks, which had been extracted from the northern and southern quarries of Tura', 'delivered within four days at the pyramid construction site'. Sheisha: 'The Journal of Merer ... describes the transport of limestone from Toura, ~17 km from the Giza Plateau, to the construction site of the Great Pyramid of Khufu.' 'Boat crew' fits transport by river; T&M also call them quarrymen, which the script does not contradict.

claims.claim: They lay buried for about four and a half thousand years.
claims.source_checked: Tallet & Marouard 2014, pp. 8, 11-12 (archive.org scan, as in 8); Sheisha et al. 2022, PMC9477388
claims.note: T&M: papyri 'deposited between the blocking stones during the last phase of occupation', found in 'the rubble filling' at gallery G1, site closed 'at the end of the reign of Khufu, ca. Year 27'; found 2013. Khufu's accession (Sheisha) 2613-2577 BCE (14C), 2589, 2554 or 2480 BCE; + 27 years gives deposit c. 2586-2453 BC, i.e. about 4,465-4,598 years before AD 2013. 'About four and a half thousand' covers all. Erdil 2025 not opened; not needed.

claims.claim: To Cleopatra, the pyramid was ancient history.
claims.note: About 2,400-2,550 years separated the building from her birth on the published chronologies. Characterisation, not a claim about what she knew.

claims.claim: We can read the work log of a crew that helped build it.
claims.source_checked: Tallet & Marouard 2014, pp. 8-11 (archive.org scan, as in 8); Sheisha et al. 2022, PMC9477388
claims.note: T&M: the logbook reports 'many operations related to the construction of the Great Pyramid of Khufu at Giza', blocks 'probably used for the external casing'; Sheisha: transport 'to the construction site of the Great Pyramid of Khufu'. 'We can read': the text is read and quoted by its excavators (T&M 2014, Fig. 14b and pp. 8-11).
